Empirical Research Plan: Minimum-Wage Hike and Fast-Food Employment

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Two–way-fixed-effects Difference-in-Differences (DID), supplemented by a restaurant-level event-study.

Justification  
• The policy creates a sharp, one-time treatment (minimum wage rises in NJ only).  
• We have panel (pre/post) data on treated and untreated units.  
• There is no obvious running variable with a manipulable cutoff, nor a credible instrument that shifts wages only through the minimum wage; hence DID is the cleanest design.  
• An event study allows us to verify the parallel-trends assumption and describe dynamics.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
Treat_i = 1 if restaurant i is located in New Jersey; 0 otherwise.

Control group  
Restaurants in eastern Pennsylvania covered by the same survey but unaffected by NJ’s policy.

Treatment timing  
Policy announced in late 1991 and implemented on 1 April 1992 (exact date can be modified if your data use a different cut).  
Post_t = 1 for observations from April 1992 onward; 0 for observations collected before that date.

DID interaction  
DID_it = Treat_i × Post_t

(If monthly data: define Post_t as months ≥ 1992-04.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of the new minimum wage, average outcomes (employment, wages, prices) in NJ and PA fast-food restaurants would have followed the same trend.  
Plausibility: States are contiguous and economically similar; short pre-period helps. We will test this via pre-trend coefficients in the event study.

A2. No spillovers/SUTVA: The policy does not change outcomes at PA restaurants (control); nor do cross-border commuting, consumer substitution, or firm relocation contaminate the counterfactual.  
Plausibility: Some workers/customers may cross the Delaware River, but fast-food demand is highly local. We can probe this by dropping border counties on either side.

A3. Stable composition: The set of restaurants surveyed pre- and post-change is comparable; openings/closings are not systematically differentially related to the policy.  
Plausibility: Surveys include chains with low exit rates in the short horizon; we will check balanced-panel robustness.

A4. No differential contemporaneous shocks: No other NJ-specific policy or macro shock hit only NJ at the same time.  
Plausibility: Check news archives and include county-level unemployment controls.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification and Mitigations
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential time trends (violation of A1).  
– Mitigation: (i) Event-study plot of pre-coefficients; (ii) allow state-specific linear trends; (iii) placebo test using 1990–1991 data if available.

T2. Cross-border spillovers (violation of A2).  
– Mitigation: (i) Exclude restaurants within, say, 10 miles of the NJ–PA border; (ii) show results are similar on both sides of PA’s interior; (iii) test for wage changes in PA restaurants.

T3. Survey measurement error and sample attrition.  
– Mitigation: (i) Use chain-level administrative payroll data if accessible; (ii) restrict to balanced panel; (iii) robustness to trimming extreme employment changes; (iv) cluster standard errors at the restaurant or county level to accommodate noise.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Libraries ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # TWFE & event-study
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data ---------------------------------------------------------------
dt <- fread("fastfood_survey.csv")   # assume one row per restaurant-month

# 2. Variable construction ---------------------------------------------------
dt[, treat := ifelse(state == "NJ", 1, 0)]
dt[, post  := ifelse(date >= as.Date("1992-04-01"), 1, 0)]
dt[, did   := treat * post]

# Event-time for event study
policy_date <- as.Date("1992-04-01")
dt[, rel_time := as.integer((date - policy_date)/30.4)]   # approx months
# collapse extreme event times
dt[rel_time < -6, rel_time := -6]
dt[rel_time >  6, rel_time :=  6]

# 3. Main TWFE DID -----------------------------------------------------------
# Outcome 1: employment (number of workers)
did_emp <- feols(emp ~ did + post + treat | restaurant_id + date, 
                 cluster = ~restaurant_id, data = dt)
summary(did_emp)

# Outcome 2: average wage
did_wage <- feols(wage ~ did + post + treat | restaurant_id + date, 
                  cluster = ~restaurant_id, data = dt)
summary(did_wage)

# 4. Event-study specification ----------------------------------------------
es_emp <- feols(emp ~ i(rel_time, treat, ref = -1) | restaurant_id + date, 
                cluster = ~restaurant_id, data = dt)
iplot(es_emp) + ggtitle("Event study: Employment")

# 5. Robustness check: drop border counties ----------------------------------
border_counties <- c("Camden","Burlington","Philadelphia","Delaware")  # example
dt_rb <- dt[!(county %in% border_counties)]
did_emp_rb <- feols(emp ~ did + post + treat | restaurant_id + date, 
                    cluster = ~restaurant_id, data = dt_rb)
etable(list(Main = did_emp, NoBorder = did_emp_rb), se.below = TRUE)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
• Wages: Large mechanical rise of roughly the statutory increase (≈ $0.40 per hour in 1992, ~10–12 %).  
• Employment: Conventional competitive-model prior is −ɛ where ɛ ≈ 0.2–0.3, implying −2 % to −3 %. Monopsony or search-friction models predict smaller, zero, or even positive effects. My prior—based on existing evidence—is a near-zero effect: point estimate around +1 % to −1 %, statistically indistinguishable from zero.  
• Prices: Slight upward adjustment (pass-through) of maybe 1–2 %.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
C1. Parallel pre-trends visually and statistically supported …………… 1  
C2. No spillovers/contamination of control group …………………………… 0.5  
C3. No differential composition changes across groups …………………… 0.5  
C4. No concurrent NJ-specific shocks ………………………………………… 1  
C5. Correct inference: clustering, serial correlation handled ………… 1  

Total (out of 5) = 4.0 → “Credible but monitor spillovers & composition.”
